stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Sweep the three sliders and watch how each one reshapes the refracted light. $\lambda$ picks the colour; $A_c$ and $B_c$ define the glass through Cauchy's law $n(\lambda) = A_c + B_c/\lambda^2$. Advance when each slider has covered at least half of its range.
stages.concept: Cauchy's dispersion law $n(\lambda) = A_c + B_c/\lambda^2$ tells us that the refractive index of a transparent material depends on the wavelength. $A_c$ sets the base index (medium averaged), and $B_c$ controls how strongly short wavelengths (blue, violet) bend more than long ones (red). The prism deviation $D = i_1 + i_2 - A$ then rides directly on $n(\lambda)$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A target exit direction $D^{*}$ is drawn as a dashed orange ray. Tune $\lambda$, $A_c$ and $B_c$ so your solid coloured exit ray becomes parallel to the target. Many parameter combinations produce the same deviation — pick any that works.
stages.concept: For fixed prism geometry ($A = 50^{\circ}$, $i_1 = 30^{\circ}$), the deviation $D$ depends only on the refractive index: $D(n) = i_1 + \arcsin\!\big(n \sin(A - \arcsin(\sin i_1 / n))\big) - A$. So any triple $(\lambda, A_c, B_c)$ that lands on the same $n$ produces the same exit direction.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The coloured rays are gone. Only the prism and the target $D^{*}$ arrow remain. Compute on paper the index $n$ that reaches $D^{*}$, then find a $(\lambda, A_c, B_c)$ triple through Cauchy's law and set the sliders. You get one submit per target.
stages.concept: Invert the deviation formula in two steps. First $D^{*} \to n$: for the fixed geometry, $n \sin(A - \arcsin(\sin i_1 / n)) = \sin(i_1 + D^{*} - A)$ — one unknown, one equation, so $n$ is unique. Then $n \to (\lambda, A_c, B_c)$ via Cauchy: fix any two of the three parameters and solve for the third.

labels.tir: total internal reflection — no exit ray
labels.tip1: sweep λ, A_c, and B_c across their ranges
labels.tip2: align your coloured exit ray with the dashed target
labels.tip3: solve n from D* on paper, then find (λ, A_c, B_c)
labels.peek_tip_formula: Rearrange: n·sin(A − arcsin(sin i₁/n)) = sin(i₁ + D* − A). Solve for n first.
labels.peek_tip_anchor: Cauchy inversion: pick λ and A_c, then B_c = (n − A_c)·(λ/1000)² μm².

1.1: Slide λ across the whole rainbow. Does the exit ray move at all when you fix A_c and B_c?
1.2: Now slide B_c from small to large with λ fixed. B_c is what makes different colours bend by different amounts — the dispersion strength.
1.3: A_c is a base offset added to every wavelength. Large A_c bends every colour more; small A_c bends every colour less. Sweep it and watch the whole ray rotate.

2.1: The target D* only depends on the index n at the current wavelength. First figure out what n produces D*.
2.2: With A = 50° and i₁ = 30°, guess n ≈ 1.51 for D ≈ 30°, n ≈ 1.60 for D ≈ 38°, n ≈ 1.66 for D ≈ 43°, n ≈ 1.71 for D ≈ 47°.
2.3: Once you know n, use Cauchy backwards: fix λ near the middle of the visible range and try A_c + B_c/(λ/1000)² ≈ n. Many triples work.

3.1: The rays are gone, but the formula still holds. Write D* = i₁ + i₂ − A on paper.
3.2: Invert Snell's law twice. With A = 50°, i₁ = 30°, compute r₁ = arcsin(sin30°/n), then r₂ = 50° − r₁, then check n·sin r₂ = sin(30° + D* − A). One unknown n.
3.3: If you peeked, you already have the numerical n. Now Cauchy: choose λ (any visible), choose A_c below n, then B_c = (n − A_c)·(λ/1000)². Set the sliders to those exact values.
